profiles.meeting_scenario: A national health technology assessment (HTA) agency is holding a design review of a draft 'Equity Framework' that is meant to accompany standard cost-effectiveness review materials during topic scoping and committee briefing. The draft has already been circulated internally, and this meeting is to judge whether the framework is sufficiently mature to move into the next stage, identify gaps in how it will be used in practice, and decide what revisions are needed before the next methods cycle. The agenda is to review the draft's structure, the section on advisory group composition, the plan for testing it on a previous HTA case, and the expected form of documentation. The expected outcome is a shared decision on whether the framework is ready for pilot use, plus a short list of revisions and owners.

members.name: Dr. Lena Morris
members.expertise: HTA process design, economic evaluation methods, committee briefing templates
members.background: Lena is a health economist who oversees methodological consistency across appraisals and is responsible for fitting new tools into the agency's existing scoping and committee workflows.
members.private_state: She wants the framework approved as a lightweight addition to the current process so it can be included in the annual methods update without triggering major retraining or delays in topic selection.
hidden_assumptions: If a framework is 'ready for pilot,' it only needs to be stable enough for internal use in one controlled live scoping exercise; external-facing language can be refined afterward.
The 'advisory group composition' part of the framework is about ensuring the right stakeholder categories are present, not about the operational supports needed for those people to participate.

When colleagues mention 'the rare disease case,' they are referring to the gene therapy appraisal used in last quarter's internal methods workshop because that is the agency's default test case for new process tools.
To 'document the rationale' means adding a concise note to the existing scoping template showing which equity prompts were considered and whether any changed the framing of the assessment.

members.name: Aisha Rahman
members.role: Equity and Public Involvement Programme Manager
members.expertise: Deliberative methods, inclusion in health policy processes, patient and community advisory structures
members.background: Aisha leads the agency's work on embedding equity and public voice into decision processes and has experience redesigning committee recruitment and consultation materials for underserved groups.
members.private_state: She wants the framework to shape actual participation and accountability, not just appear in methods paperwork, and hopes this review will lock in stronger implementation expectations before the tool becomes routinized.
hidden_assumptions: If a framework is 'ready for pilot,' it is polished enough to share with patient and lay advisors for reaction before being used in a live assessment setting.

The 'advisory group composition' section naturally includes the practical participation conditions—translation, honoraria, accessibility supports, and meeting format—that determine who can really be in the room.

When people refer to 'the rare disease case,' they mean the pediatric spinal muscular atrophy appraisal that community partners repeatedly cited in equity consultations as the clearest example of uneven burden.

To 'document the rationale' means maintaining a traceable record across scoping, evidence review, and committee deliberation so future reviewers can see how equity considerations were addressed or set aside.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the framework may be 'ready for pilot.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the draft is sufficiently stable for an internal trial in one upcoming scoping meeting, even if wording and usability details are still rough for external audiences.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the draft is mature enough to circulate to patient/public advisors and then test in a live setting with those external users involved.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design review settings, 'pilot' is a routine next-step label that usually signals progress rather than a need to define audience or readiness threshold, so both hear confirmation without probing its operational meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'advisory group composition' section
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the draft needs a stronger section on 'advisory group composition.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this section should clarify which expertise and stakeholder categories must be represented when the HTA is scoped or discussed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this section should also cover the enabling conditions for participation, such as interpreters, childcare reimbursement, honoraria, remote access, and readable materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds broad and self-explanatory, and both participants support inclusion, so the hidden disagreement over where the boundary of the section lies never feels like a disagreement.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'rare disease case' will be used as the test example
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the rare disease case' as the obvious example for trying the framework.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the recently reviewed gene therapy appraisal used internally because the documentation is complete and already mapped to standard HTA templates.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the earlier pediatric spinal muscular atrophy appraisal because it surfaced community access issues and is familiar to the external advisors she works with.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both examples are prominent rare disease appraisals at the agency and both plausibly illustrate equity concerns, so shorthand reference to 'the rare disease case' feels unambiguous even though each has a different case in mind.

misalignment_points.topic: How much traceability is meant by 'document the rationale'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the framework should 'document the rationale' for equity-related judgments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this requirement is met by a short summary in the scoping or briefing template noting the relevant prompts and any resulting change in framing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this requires an auditable decision trail showing where equity issues were raised, what evidence was sought, who commented, and why some concerns did not alter the final recommendation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Documentation is universally seen as good practice, and both are trying to be practical, so the difference in what counts as adequate evidence of reasoning remains hidden behind shared approval of the phrase.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this moving toward approval in the methods update. For me, ready for pilot means the draft is stable enough to run once in a controlled internal scoping exercise, not that every phrase is polished for external audiences. If we can limit today's outcome to a short revision list, we avoid opening up a bigger redesign or retraining discussion.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. What I'd like to do today is confirm whether the equity framework is ready for pilot and, if so, pin down only the revisions we need before it goes into the next methods cycle.

turns.inner_thought: This is the moment to make sure the framework is strong enough to be seen by patient and lay advisors before it gets embedded as just another internal form. If it's ready for pilot, it should be mature enough that external people can react to it without feeling they've been handed a rough internal draft.
turns.utterance: I think it's very promising. If we are saying it's ready for pilot, I'd just want to make sure the language works for lay advisors as well as for internal staff.

turns.inner_thought: The section that most needs tightening is the advisory group composition part. Topic teams will need clearer prompts on which stakeholder categories and types of expertise should be around the table at scoping. If that is sharper, it will sit neatly alongside current scoping practice.
turns.utterance: One area I'd especially focus on is advisory group composition. I think that section could be tightened so topic teams are clearer about which voices need to be represented at scoping.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and that section has to do more than name categories. Advisory group composition should also imply the practical conditions that make participation real: interpretation, honoraria, accessible formats, remote options, readable papers. If we don't build that in now, the framework will look inclusive on paper and exclude people in practice.
turns.utterance: I agree. The draft does need a stronger section on advisory group composition, and I think it should help teams think about what makes participation actually feasible, not just who ought to be there.

turns.inner_thought: For the test run, the rare disease case is the obvious one: the gene therapy appraisal from the workshop already has complete documentation and maps cleanly onto our standard templates. That makes it efficient for seeing whether the prompts fit the scoping and briefing materials without a lot of reconstruction work.
turns.utterance: On testing, my instinct is that the rare disease case is the obvious place to start. The files are clean, and it should give us a straightforward read on whether the prompts fit with the current templates.

turns.inner_thought: Good, the rare disease case should work well because the SMA appraisal is exactly the one community partners kept raising in the equity consultations. If we use that example, external advisors will immediately recognise why the framework matters and can respond to it from lived experience rather than abstraction.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think the rare disease case makes sense. It will also resonate with the external people who discussed that example during the earlier equity consultations.

turns.inner_thought: I need to head off any expectation of creating a new audit system. Document the rationale should mean a concise note in the existing scoping and briefing fields showing which prompts were considered and whether any changed the framing. If this turns into a full traceability exercise, topic teams will resist it and we'll miss the methods cycle.
turns.utterance: The one thing I'd be cautious about is creating a heavy reporting burden. I absolutely agree we should document the rationale, but my preference would be to do that within the existing scoping and briefing fields rather than build a separate layer around it.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want a token note that disappears into a template. Document the rationale needs to mean a traceable record across stages so later committees and reviewers can see what equity issues were raised, who commented, what evidence was sought, and why some concerns did or didn't change the outcome. But I can frame that as continuity rather than extra burden.
turns.utterance: I agree with keeping it proportionate, and I do think the rationale needs to be documented clearly enough that future committees can see how equity issues were considered and what happened to concerns that were raised.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds aligned enough to close. I'll summarise a tight package: sharpen advisory group composition, sense-check the framework on the rare disease case, then move into pilot. If we keep it framed that way, we can get this into the annual update without reopening the whole process design.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. So, as I hear it, the main revisions are to polish the advisory group composition section, check the framework against the rare disease case, and then move it into pilot.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with that summary as long as the next step doesn't narrow the ambition. If the rationale is documented properly and the pilot includes meaningful external input, we'll have a defensible basis for asking for stronger implementation later instead of letting this become just another internal checklist.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works for me. If we make sure the rationale is documented clearly, the pilot should give us a solid basis for a broader rollout afterward.
